title: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Services, Inc. (2005)
summary: Section 1367 permitted related claims below the diversity amount threshold when an anchor claim satisfied that threshold and there was no other jurisdictional defect.
notes:
Separate claim aggregation from supplemental jurisdiction. The case does not combine small claims into one fictional large claim; it identifies a valid anchor and asks whether the statute supplies authority over additional related claims.

The two consolidated cases were the Exxon dealers' class action (about 10,000 dealers alleging fuel overcharges, where the Eleventh Circuit upheld supplemental jurisdiction after a jury verdict) and Ortega v. Star-Kist (a nine-year-old injured by a tuna can, where only her claim met the amount and the First Circuit rejected jurisdiction over her family's claims); the Court (Kennedy, J.) affirmed the Eleventh Circuit and reversed the First Circuit.

The majority distinguished incomplete diversity, which 'contaminates' the whole action and so is not cured by § 1367, from a single plaintiff's failure to meet the amount in controversy, which does not.

sections.Parties: The consolidated matters involved Exxon dealers asserting related claims and a separate family action arising from an injury. Some plaintiffs’ claims satisfied the jurisdictional amount; others did not.
sections.Material Facts: The original claims supplied diversity jurisdiction, with complete diversity of citizenship and at least one claim meeting the amount requirement. The additional plaintiffs’ claims were part of the same constitutional controversy but fell below the monetary threshold. The question was whether § 1367 extended jurisdiction to those claims despite older rules requiring each claimant to meet the amount.
sections.Procedural History: The consolidated cases reached the Supreme Court after differing jurisdictional treatment. The Court held, five to four, that § 1367 authorized the additional claims in the circumstances presented.
sections.Issue: Does § 1367 extend to related claims that fall below the amount requirement when the action otherwise has a valid diversity foundation?
sections.Holding: Yes, subject to the statute’s requirements and exceptions. The statute displaced the earlier amount rule applicable to the claims at issue.
sections.Reasoning: The majority read subsection (a) to authorize supplemental jurisdiction over claims forming part of the same Article III case once the court had original jurisdiction over a qualifying claim. It then examined the exclusions in subsection (b), including Congress’s treatment of particular joinder rules. The relevant additional claims were not excluded merely because their amounts were smaller. A failure of complete diversity was different: introducing a nondiverse party could undermine the original diversity basis itself. The Court therefore did not permit every claim to ride along with a large claim. Relatedness, the original jurisdictional foundation, and each statutory exclusion still had to be addressed.

learning.why: Section 1367 permitted related claims below the diversity amount threshold when an anchor claim satisfied that threshold and there was no other jurisdictional defect.

topics.cp-supplemental-diversity: Section 1367 could include related claims below the amount threshold when at least one claim met it and complete diversity remained.
topics.cp-amount-in-controversy: The amount defect of additional claims was treated differently from the presence of a nondiverse party.
topics.cp-class-jurisdiction: The Court applied the statute to claims of class members as well as the consolidated multi-plaintiff setting.
topics.cp-statute-interpretation: The majority’s reading of subsections (a) and (b) differs from the dissent’s use of prior doctrine and statutory context.
topics.cp-usc-1367: The case is the leading construction of § 1367(a) and (b) for diversity cases.
topics.cp-aggregation: It resolves whether plaintiffs with claims below the threshold may ride along with one plaintiff who meets it, the modern aggregation question.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Ginsburg’s dissent, joined by three Justices, read the statute against the background of prior diversity doctrine and disputed the majority’s interpretation. Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Breyer, also emphasized legislative history.
